title: Democrats Won Congress. For H-1B Holders, the Rules Still Run Through Agencies and Courts
excerpt: Almost every H-1B and PERM restriction since September 2025 came from the White House and federal agencies — and a midterm win does not repeal an agency rule.
body:
• Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the November 3 midterms, according to USA Today and Associated Press calls — but the new Congress does not sit until January 3, 2027.
  • Nothing changes automatically for H-1B holders: the $100,000 fee extension to September 21, 2027, the wage-weighted lottery and the proposed $103,265 petition fee are executive and agency actions, not laws Congress passed.
  • To overturn a final agency rule, Congress must pass a law and survive a presidential veto — an override needs two-thirds of both chambers, which Democrats do not have.
  • What the majority does control: the Labor Department budget that funds PERM analysts, committee oversight of DHS, and Senate confirmation of the judges who decide immigration cases.

Democrats have won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the US midterm elections held on November 3, according to USA Today's election coverage. For Indian professionals, an analysis published by TradingView News argues, the result changes less than the headlines suggest — because almost every restriction on H-1B and PERM since September 2025 came from the White House and federal agencies, and winning an election does not repeal an agency rule.

Who is affected, and what is actually in force

The restrictions bearing on H-1B workers are executive and regulatory. On September 18, President Donald Trump extended the $100,000 H-1B payment to September 21, 2027, and signed an executive order asking agencies to weigh an employer's layoffs when deciding petitions. The Department of Homeland Security replaced the random H-1B lottery with a wage-weighted selection from February 27. The Department of Labor has proposed raising the four prevailing wage levels from the 17th, 34th, 50th and 67th percentiles to the 34th, 52nd, 70th and 88th — adding about $14,000, or ₹13.3 lakh, to the average certified wage by the department's own estimate. DHS has separately proposed a fee of $103,265, close to ₹1 crore, on every cap-subject petition, and a further proposal would end the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers who lose their jobs.

The demand side has already shifted. USCIS received 211,600 H-1B registrations for fiscal 2027, down 38.5 per cent from 343,981 a year earlier, and only 17.7 per cent of those selected were at the entry wage level. A Congressional Research Service report of October 14 shows Infosys cut its registrations by 91 per cent and Tata Consultancy Services by 95 per cent, while Cognizant filed none.

Why Congress cannot simply undo it

The new Congress sits from January 3, 2027. To overturn a final rule, Congress must pass a law; the President holds a veto, and an override needs two-thirds of both chambers. Democrats do not have those numbers. The courts, meanwhile, have done more than legislators to slow the hardest measure: a Massachusetts district court vacated the $100,000 fee on June 8, the First Circuit refused on July 24 to restore it, and a California district court blocked the fee a second time on September 30. A Washington DC court upheld the fee in December 2025; that ruling is also on appeal.

What the majority can do — and what to do now

The levers Democrats do hold are real but slow. They will write the Labor Department's budget, which pays for the analysts who clear the PERM queue — as of October 5, the department was reviewing PERM applications filed in December 2025, with an average analyst review of 336 days. They will control the committees that can summon DHS officials to explain the $103,265 fee. The Senate confirms the federal judges who decide immigration disputes. And no new restrictive H-1B bill can pass without Democratic votes — though the analysis cautions that a Democratic Congress is no automatic friend of H-1B: the H-1B and L-1 Visa Reform Act is co-sponsored by Democrat Dick Durbin alongside Republican Chuck Grassley, and would raise wage floors and bar petitions for positions where American workers were laid off within 180 days.

The deepest problem is statutory. The 7 per cent per-country limit on employment-based green cards is written into law, and the November 2026 Visa Bulletin holds the EB-2 final action date for India at November 1, 2013 — a 13-year wait. Workers born in India received 71 per cent of approved H-1B petitions in fiscal 2024, according to USCIS. For applicants, the practical instruction is unchanged: file to the rules as they stand, watch the appellate decisions on the $100,000 fee, and treat January 3, 2027 — not election night — as the date congressional leverage begins.
